basemap.ground_at and terrain_tile take the finest of: a bundled fine grid (the packs: Israel at 139 m) → the user's elevation files (SRTM .hgt, 1201² = 3" or 3601² = 1", in ~/.signalviewer/terrain/ or the folder chosen in Settings; read with numpy) → terrarium tiles (Mapzen / AWS open data: SRTM, GMTED2010, ETOPO1; level 12, ~30 m), fetched only when the network is allowed (not Never use the network, no SV_OFFLINE) and kept in the tile cache with the same rules as online map tiles → the bundled world grid (11 km). A fetch runs in the background: the answer comes from what is there, and /api/terrain/version changes when finer heights arrived (the app's 3D view then asks its terrain again; the tile URLs carry the version so the browser's cache does not keep the coarse one). basemap.step_at(lat, lon) is the step of the best source at a point, never fetching.

The offline 3D page says what its ground is: the footer always ("terrain: 139 m grid"), and a line over the scene when the step at its centre is over 1 km. Its ground reaches the horizon: the near mesh (the tracks' box, 129 × 129) over a far one (8 × its side, 40 to 200 km, 129 × 129, 2 m lower and not drawn inside the near box), fog from 0.6 × to 1.4 × the far side, a sky gradient, the sun 35° high from the north-west. Heights ×1 by default (honest), ×2 / ×5 / ×10; "flat here" beside the choice when the relief is under 4 % of the near side. The PDF / Word / PNG picture draws the far ground as far as twice the near box. The page is a flat local frame: Earth's curvature is not drawn (at 100 km it would drop the horizon by ~800 m).

docs.title: Hiding an object (P6, 1.26)
docs.text: One rule: a hidden object (MapObject.hidden) is not drawn, not part of Fit, and keeps its place in the list (greyed, struck through). shownObjects(plot) (mapObjects.ts) is what the drawing loops of Globe3D.tsx and GeoChart.tsx iterate (their track fetch, models, markers, labels, tracks, Fit); lookups of another object (a borrowed attitude, the pair) use the whole list. A hidden one of the pair shows "— hidden —" in the relation box; a camera on it goes to Free. Pictures skip it; the offline pages start with it hidden and their legend rows are buttons (svLegend in report_assets/relation.js; click, Alt+click = only this one). Exports (Tacview, CSV, KML) keep every object.

docs.title: The Map is 3D (P4, 1.26)
docs.text:
One Map, and it is the 3D view. Saved values do not change: mode: "geo" with objects is drawn by the 3D view (isMapPlot, mapObjects.ts); mode: "3d" as before; new maps are "3d". Two cameras (owner, 2026-11-16: "enough to mark whether the camera is free or on the object"): Free, or On the object (followObject set) - the camera stays on it, a drag turns around it, the wheel / + − go towards the object itself down to 1 m, sitting on it (within 15 m its own model and any within 20 m of it are hidden). mapCamera reads every older camera value ("top", "chase", "cockpit", "lookat") by followObject alone, so a session opens On the object when it followed one, else Free; Free writes camera: "free", On the object clears it. From above, Around it, Behind it, Cockpit, Look at (1.26-1.27) are gone; the 2D drawing's track up is its N button (mapUp). with the same camera as before. A 1.25 build opening a session from this one draws its maps as before. mode: "geo" without objects - a lon / lat X-Y on a map - is unchanged (GeoChart).

When 3D cannot draw (hasWebGL() false - webgl.ts, no CesiumJS loaded for the check - or the context lost) the Map is drawn by GeoChart with "Shown flat – this computer cannot draw 3D" and the same bar. Globe3DFallback.tsx (tracks on bare axes) is gone. ui.mapFlat forces the flat drawing (P8's Map drawing: Always flat; the flat-map e2e tests use it implicitly - their browser has no WebGL).

Reports and pages: a Map goes out as the 3D view on its camera (plotSpec → mode: "3d", scene.camera: "centre" On the object, else "free") → scene3d.render; the live page opens on that camera (D.camera). (report._map_picture's flat picture for "top" is no longer asked for by the app.) The flat page (map.html) inside the 3D page's frame for a browser without WebGL is not done (the page shows its picture there, as before).

2D feature where it was (GeoChart.tsx) where it is now the mouse's position .geo-readout (lat / lon) Globe3D.tsx .g3-readout: lat / lon (decimals by the camera's height), ground height, distance / bearing from the reference (scene.globe.pick, one update a frame) - e2e test_the_map_from_above_and_the_mouse_readout north up / track up mapUp the flat drawing On the object: the N button turns the map with the object and back north ring tooltips ringTip the 3D rings and their hover (1.26, existing) relation lines and distance relation layer existing in 3D (relLines) - test_globe3d related-objects test track colouring by a value trackColors existing in 3D (objColors) object dialog from a click marker click existing in 3D (a click on a model) back to the object after a drag followOff 3D: drag while following orbits around it (no button needed) - note: not identical keyboard + − 0, arrows key handler + − 0 in the bar; arrows: not in 3D yet (note) offline basemap / online imagery geoBase existing in 3D (the same Map background picker) hover on a track point track hover existing in 3D (Readout box) the mouse's position in the offline 3D page - not done (the page's hover shows track points; the ground raycast is left)

docs.title: Places (P7, 1.26)
docs.text:
Named points, lines and areas on every Map, and saved camera views. Two lists: Places of this session (Workspace.places, saved with the session and with a template made from it) and My places (the user's own, in every session - the app keeps them in ~/.signalviewer/places.json, a file that can be given to a colleague). One panel holds them (the Map's ⋯ → Places…); the command palette has Go to a place… and Add a place….

  • Positions are read by one parser (svcore/places.py parse_coords): decimal degrees ("32.687, 35.39") or degrees-minutes-seconds (32°41'13"N 35°23'24"E, N32 41 13 E35 23 24); without hemisphere letters the order is latitude, longitude. A new point's height is the ground there (/api/ground).
  • Import: .kml (points, lines, polygons - their outer ring), .kmz (the zip's KML), .geojson (Point / LineString / Polygon and their Multi- forms), .csv (name, lat, lon[, alt], a header optional; degrees-minutes-seconds in the cells work). A shape with no valid position is left out and counted.
  • Drawing: in 3D a point is its icon on a thin 30 m pole with its name; lines and areas are draped on the ground (Cesium ground primitives) - in the software-WebGL light mode, for the frame rate, plain lines 2 m over the ground under each vertex. The flat drawing, both offline pages and the pictures draw the same shapes. Places take part in Fit only when the Map has no objects.
  • Readout and relation: the mouse readout adds the nearest shown place within 50 km; the relation box's Compared with list ends with the places (Plot.relPlace; a place is a fixed point).
  • Exports: the KML file holds every shown place (a saved view as a LookAt); the ACMI file holds the points as stationary objects - Type=Navaid+Static+Waypoint, an airfield Ground+Static+Aerodrome (both from the ACMI 2.2 type list).

docs.title: Settings > Map and objects (P8, 1.26)
docs.text:
One module reads and writes these settings (frontend/src/mapDefaults.ts, keys sv3.map.*). They apply to new things only - a new object, a new Map, the next export; an open session, a template or an object already made is never changed by them. Drawn things (names, the track's width, units, coordinates) follow the setting at once, in the app and in the pages and pictures made after.

Setting Choices (default first) Icon of a new object, per class (truth / navigation / receiver / other) aircraft · uav · drone · missile · ship · vehicle Camera of a new Map Free · On the object (an older Behind it reads as On the object, From above as Free) Map drawing Automatic · Always flat (light) Relation box on a new Map / Names on the Map shown · hidden Track width 2.5 px · 1.5 · 4 Model size of a new object medium (26) · small (18) · large (36) Distances and heights m / km · ft / NM (below 1 NM in feet) Coordinates decimal degrees · degrees-minutes-seconds · MGRS (80° S to 84° N; the polar grid is not done) Elevation files a folder of SRTM .hgt files (empty: ~/.signalviewer/terrain) Export rate for Tacview / KML 10 · 5 · 2 · 1 samples a second Story on · off; about 90 s · 45 s · 3 min

docs.title: The wow (P9, 1.26)
docs.text:
• Light: the sun where it was - the recording's own time when its times are Unix dates, else 10:00 local solar time at an equinox (scene3d.sun_position, NOAA's low-precision formulas, ~0.5°). The app: sky atmosphere, lighting, fog; soft model shadows only while the camera is on an object.
  • In space: a drop line and a dark disc under each object; its last 10 s brighter over the whole track.
  • Flights: every camera change eases there over ~1.2 s (none with the system's reduce motion).
  • On it: On the object zoomed all the way in (within 15 m) hides its own model (and any within 20 m) - the view from the object, turned by a drag (Cockpit until 2026-11-16).
  • Flight display (Display in the bar, On the object) and a mini-map while the camera is near an object (a click flies there).
  • The error, drawn: when the relation box's pair is one vehicle (median distance under 20 m) a see-through surface between the tracks, green → amber → red at the distance's 95th percentile, with its scale and a toggle in the relation box. The app draws it while the camera is within 3 km (from further it is under a pixel); the flat drawing colours the compared track instead.
  • Light mode (software WebGL): sky, shadows, drop lines, the 10 s trail and the error surface are off; the display, mini-map, cockpit and flights stay (no GPU cost).

docs.title: Story mode (P10, 1.26)
docs.text: svcore/story.py picks the moments: the page's marks (the log's errors and warnings, health findings, the user's notes) and, from the reference object of the tab's first Map, takeoff / landing (the height above the ground crossing 5 m for 3 s), the highest and fastest points, the steepest bank (over 30°), passing within 200 m of a place, and for the pair the largest error (one vehicle) or the closest and farthest moments. A moment within 3 s of a stronger one is dropped; at most 12. The live page's player runs the time so the recording takes about the Settings' length (×1 to ×60), at ×1 from 3 s before a moment to 2 s after, and stops 4 s on it; the map frames fly to its object (the offline pages: Around it ~400 m; Behind it for a bank, an error, a takeoff or a landing) and give the reader's camera back at the end.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Measured with tools/benchmark.py on a 1-CPU, 4 GB test machine (full results in docs/). The first-open target is scaled by the number of values (5 s per 40 M values, the reference file).

5 M rows × 7 (730 MB) 20 M rows × 4 (1.7 GB) 5,000 rows × 5,000 columns (262 MB) Open, first time 4.2 – 4.8 s (target 5.0) 12.2 s (target 12.5) 3.6 s (target 3.1) Open again (cache) 0.07 s 0.06 s 0.44 s Memory for the data 1.07× binary size 1.03× 0.12× (only shown columns are read) Redraw full / zoom / deep zoom 6 / 9 / 5 ms 6 / 11 / 6 ms 5 / 4 / 4 ms Cursor values 1 ms 1 ms 1 ms Live mode, 1,000 new rows 149 ms 295 ms 741 ms

Parsing runs at about 8.5 M values per second per CPU core for both long and wide files and scales with cores (64 MB parts are parsed in parallel). Redraw time does not grow with file size: min/max summaries per 1,024-sample block are computed once per signal. Wide files: the cache is one column-major matrix (not one file per column), discrete-signal detection runs on demand, the signal list is virtualized, and signal choosers are searchable instead of long dropdowns.

docs.text:
Generated data, no file needed (--samples, default 5 million per signal; --json writes the numbers; --check SLACK exits 1 when a target is missed - times may be SLACK times their target, sizes not - which CI runs with --samples 2000000 --check 3). Measured on a 2-CPU test machine:

Measurement Target Result Plot request with a run time offset / without (one signal, zoomed) ≤ 2× 0.97× (3.2 / 3.3 ms; was ~15× before 1.23) Zoom step, 30 signals (server, binary answer) < 500 ms 17 ms Data sent for that step ≤ 2 MB 1.4 MB (JSON before 1.23: a third more) Pan burst of 10 steps: the last answer (older ones cancelled) < 300 ms 19 ms (186 ms when every step was waited for) Large .bin (52 MB) with 10 changed signals: memory cache / its budget ≤ 1 59 / 1024 MB Live append, 300-column CSV: 1,000 rows readable < 1 s 35 ms

Opening several files at once (1.23): four 55 MB ArduPilot logs in 1.4 s instead of 2.1 s on two cores.

docs.title: Simulation against flight
docs.text:
A worked example from start to finish: the same attitude test flown in a model and on the vehicle, lined up in time, compared signal by signal, and turned into a pass / fail check for CI.

The files are in examples/sim_vs_flight/ (and on the welcome screen: a simulation against its flight); tools/make_sim_vs_flight.py writes them and says exactly what was put in.

File What it is sim_attitude_doublets.mat the model, as a Simulink run logs it: tout, ATT.*, RATE.* – 100 Hz, from 0 s flight_attitude_doublets.bin the vehicle: an ArduPilot log – ATT / RATE at 50 Hz, IMU at 250 Hz, flight modes; time from boot tolerances.json the limits for the command line

The test. In ALT_HOLD the pilot flies roll doublets (10°, 15°, 20°) and then pitch doublets – the usual way to check an attitude loop against its model. Both sides follow the same commands. Hidden in the flight, for you to find: the vehicle's roll is less damped than the model's, it answers 25 ms later, and its IMU carries an 82 Hz motor vibration the model does not have.

docs.title: 1. Open both files
docs.text:
Open the two files together (or click the example). Signals of the same quantity are paired across the files even though the names differ by their unit – the .mat says ATT.Roll, the log ATT.Roll [deg] – and the start card offers Compare open files.

The doublets are there twice: the simulation counts from 0 s, the log from the autopilot's boot.

docs.title: 2. Align them in time
docs.text:
Right-click the flight file → Align time with another file…. The model is the reference (it keeps its time); the flight is shifted onto it. The app correlates the commands both sides share and proposes −104.369 s, correlation 0.998 (the test really began 104.37 s after boot).

Apply: the doublets now lie on top of each other, and the offset shows next to the file (−104.4s). Align on a command (DesRoll), not on a response: a response carries the vehicle's own delay, which is one of the things you want to measure, not to remove.

docs.title: 3. Look closer
docs.text: Drag over the 20° roll doublet. The commands coincide; the model settles at ±20°, the vehicle overshoots to about −24° and rings once – lower damping than the model assumed. Pitch, a few plots down, follows the model.

docs.title: 4. Rank every signal
docs.text:
Compare runs (side bar), against the simulation: every signal both files have, least similar first, with a small curve of where in time they differ. The roll rate and roll angle differ at each doublet; the commands and yaw are the same; the rates are noisier in flight (a derivative of a noisy angle). Table of all signals gives the numbers; Export CSV takes them away.

More from here, all in the app:

  • A − B (Create signals → two signals) – the difference itself, and how far apart the two are in each flight mode.
  • Spectrum of IMU[0].AccZ – the 82 Hz line the model never had (FFT mode on the plot).
  • The same segment of each run, when several flights are compared (Compare over → A segment).

docs.title: 5. The same check in CI
docs.text:
signalviewer-cli compare sim_attitude_doublets.mat flight_attitude_doublets.bin \
    --align auto --align-on ATT.DesRoll --tolerances tolerances.json

flight_attitude_doublets.bin  vs  sim_attitude_doublets.mat
        (time alignment)  - flight_attitude_doublets.bin moved by -104.369 s (correlation 0.998 on ATT.DesRoll)
  FAIL  RATE.R  - 0.089 % of samples outside ±30.0; RMS 5.598 (4.04 % of range), max |Δ| 39.32, r 0.917
  FAIL  ATT.Roll  - 1.4 % of samples outside ±3.0; RMS 0.7111 (1.76 % of range), max |Δ| 6.065, r 0.993
  ... 5 more (--top 0 shows all)
5 passed, 2 failed, 0 errors, 0 skipped

Exit code 1: the roll loop is outside the model's tolerance – exactly the finding above; pitch, the commands and yaw pass (--top 0 lists them). What the command does:

  • --align auto lines the flight up with the model by cross-correlation (the app's Align); --align-on picks the signal (default: the best-correlated of the compared ones); --align -104.37 gives the shift yourself. Name the signal in CI: a limit on every single sample is sensitive to tens of milliseconds of shift, and the default may pick another signal as the data changes (here ATT.Pitch: 26 ms away, and the commands ATT.DesRoll and ATT.DesPitch fail too).
  • Names match with or without their unit. Where they differ otherwise, pair them in the tolerances: "signals": {"phi": {"as": "ATT.Roll", "abs": 3}}.
  • tolerances.json sets the limits: "default": {"abs": 3.0} for every signal, larger for the rates, "skip": true for what is not compared. --junit report.xml for the CI's test view.
  • A few samples outside can be allowed: "outside_pct": 0.5 (per signal or in default) or --allow-outside 0.5 passes a signal when at most 0.5 % of its samples are outside - for a spike at a step that is not the finding. Here RATE.R (0.089 % outside) would then pass and ATT.Roll (1.4 %) would still fail.

The numbers in the output above may differ in the last digits on your machine; the verdict does not.

docs.title: הדגמת הסריקה החכמה – לראות אותה מתכנסת על המחשב שלכם
docs.text: מסך הפתיחה ← הדגמת סריקה חכמה. בפחות מדקה על מחשב נייד רגיל רואים את הלולאה של הרצות הבאות ומצב Launcher מוצאת הגברים ששלושה רחפנים יכולים לחלוק – וכמה זה חוסך לעומת הרצת כל הרשת.

docs.title: מה רואים
docs.text:
• הסימולציה היא תוכנה אמיתית (examples/smart_sweep_demo/sim.py, ספרייה סטנדרטית בלבד): קוראת קובץ פרמטרים JSON וכותבת שורת CSV אחת בשם ההרצה. היא רצה על מאגר עובדים מקומי – רואים אותם מתמלאים ומתרוקנים.
  • סבב 1 מריץ רשת התחלה גסה (4 × 4 × 4 ערכי הגבר × התרחישים של כל רחפן: 768 הרצות).
  • כל סבב הבא מציע 20 ערכים מועמדים (× 12 הרצות) היכן שהם עוזרים הכי הרבה.
  • הייחוס הוא כל הרשת העדינה (9,261 ערכים × 12 = 111,132 הרצות), מחושב פעם אחת בזיכרון – רק למדידה.

docs.title: איך לקרוא
docs.text:
• גרף ההתכנסות: x = הרצות שבוצעו, y = זמן ההתייצבות הטוב ביותר (של הרחפן הגרוע) עד כה; הקו המקווקו הוא האופטימום של הרשת המלאה; הסמן מימין – היכן הרשת המלאה הייתה מסתיימת.
  • מרחב ההגברים: שניים משלושת ההגברים על הצירים (השלישי בסרגל); הערכים שנוסו צבועים לפי סבב; הטוב הנוכחי; האופטימום האמיתי כטבעת.
  • המשפט מחושב מהמספרים.

סבב הבא, הרץ עד התכנסות (נעצר כשהטוב לא השתנה שני סבבים, כשאין מה להציע, או במגבלת הסבבים), אפס.

docs.title: בלי האפליקציה
docs.text: python -m signalviewer.study demo examples/smart_sweep_demo/demo.svstudy.json

docs.title: הלולאה – אותה לולאה גם לתוכנה שלכם
docs.text:
ההדגמה היא מקרה אחד של הלולאה, שכל מחקר ב-Sweeps יכול להריץ (עמודת הרצה בצד שלו: סבב הבא, הרץ עד התכנסות, עצור):

  1. Signal Viewer מציע את ההרצות הבאות (ההגברים לנסות, לכל אחד הסיבה);
  2. הוא כותב קובץ פרמטרים לכל הרצה ומפעיל את הפקודה של המחקר – התוכנה שלכם על המחשב הזה או ה-launcher של החווה;
  3. הוא ממתין לקבצי התוצאה בתיקיית התוצאות וקורא אותם;
  4. הוא מדרג את כל הערכים שנוסו ומציע שוב – עד שהטוב לא השתנה שני סבבים, אין מה לנסות, או מגבלת הסבבים.

עמודת ההרצה מראה מה הסבב הבא יריץ, את הפקודה המדויקת, את ההרצות שבוצעו / רצות / נכשלו, את הטוב עד כה ואת ההתכנסות; כל סבב מופיע מתחת לטבלה שלו בנווט של המחקר (חדשים מסומנים) ונפתח כמו הטבלה הזו.

docs.title: להפוך אותה לשלכם
docs.text: בהדגמה, על המחקר הזה (בנווט) ← העתק את ההדגמה לתיקייה… מעתיק את המחקר ואת sim.py לתיקייה חדשה ופותח אותה כמחקר, בלי שום הרצה. שם, בשליחת ריצות (שלב הנתונים) ← איך מריצים: הפקודה לריצה אחת (ארגומנט בכל שורה, למשל python · {{study_dir}}/my_sim.py · {{params_file}}), היכן היא רצה (המחשב הזה או משגר החווה), היכן מופיעות התוצאות, ותבנית קובץ הפרמטרים של כל טבלה. ואז סבב הבא או הרץ עד התכנסות בעמודת ההרצה. אם אף הרצה בסבב לא הניבה תוצאה, הלולאה נעצרת ומציגה את סוף הפלט של הפקודה.

docs.title: התוכנה שלכם
docs.text: שמרו על החוזה – לקרוא את קובץ הפרמטרים, לכתוב שורת CSV אחת היכן ש-out אומר – ושנו את launcher.submit. כדי להריץ על החווה – שנו את בלוק ה-launcher (ראו מצב Launcher).

docs.title: The smart-sweep demo – see it converge on your PC
docs.text: Welcome → Smart sweep demo. In under a minute on an ordinary laptop, watch the loop of Next runs to try and Launcher mode find the gains three drones can share – and see what it saves compared with running the whole grid.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• The simulation is a real program (examples/smart_sweep_demo/sim.py, standard library only): it reads one JSON parameters file and writes one CSV row named by the run. It is run on a local pool of workers – you see them fill and empty.
  • Round 1 runs a coarse start grid (4 × 4 × 4 gain values × each drone's scenarios: 768 runs).
  • Each next round proposes 20 candidate values (× 12 runs) where they help most: around the best, at the edge of the constraints, where a drone has not run.
  • The reference is the whole fine grid (21 × 21 × 21 = 9 261 values × 12 = 111 132 runs) computed once in memory with the same formulas – only to measure, never to propose.

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
• The convergence chart: x = runs executed, y = the best (worst-drone) settling time found so far; the dashed line is the full-grid optimum; the marker at the right is where the full grid would finish.
  • The gain space: two of the three gains on the axes (the third on the slider); the values tried, coloured by round, filled when they hold for every drone; the current best; the true optimum as a ring.
  • The sentence is computed from the numbers, e.g. "Found the full-grid optimum within 0.5 % after 1 728 runs – the full grid needs 9 261 × 12 = 111 132 runs (≈ 64× fewer)."

Next round runs one round; Run until converged stops when the best has not changed for two rounds, when nothing is left to propose, or at the round limit; Reset starts again. It runs in ~/.signalviewer/ smart_sweep_demo, never in the installed examples.

docs.title: Without the app
docs.text:
python -m signalviewer.study demo examples/smart_sweep_demo/demo.svstudy.json

prints one line per round (runs, best, gap to the full-grid optimum) and the same sentence.

docs.title: The loop – the same for your own program
docs.text:
The demo is one case of the loop, which any study in Sweeps can run (the Run column on its right: Next round, Run until converged, Stop):

  1. Signal Viewer proposes the next runs (the gains to try, each with its reason);
  2. it writes one parameters file per run and starts the command of the study – your program on this PC (on this PC, N runs at a time) or your farm's launcher;
  3. it waits for the result files to appear in the results folder (results/{{table}}/{{run_id}}*), reads them;
  4. it ranks every value tried so far and proposes again – until the best has not changed for two rounds, nothing is left to try, or the round limit. Stop stops after the running round; the loop can be started again later.

The demo opens on Next runs: it shows what the next round will run, the exact command, the runs done / running / failed, the best so far and the convergence; each round is listed under its table in the Data step (new ones marked) and opens as that table.

docs.title: Make it yours
docs.text:
In the demo, About this study (in the Data step) → Copy the demo to a folder… copies the study and sim.py into a new folder and opens it as a study, nothing run yet. There, in Data → Send runs → How to run:

  • The command for one run – one argument per line, run without a shell, e.g. python · {{study_dir}}/my_sim.py · {{params_file}} ({{study_dir}} is the study's folder; the command runs in the round's folder);
  • Where it runs – This PC (how many at the same time) or Farm launcher (once per round with a list file, or once per run);
  • Results – where a run's result file appears;
  • each table's parameters file – a template with {{column}} placeholders.

Then Next round or Run until converged beside it. If no run of a round gives a result, the loop stops and shows the end of the command's output.

docs.title: Your own program
docs.text: Keep the contract – read the parameters file, write one CSV row (inputs, outputs, run_id) where out says – and change the study's launcher.submit to run it, e.g. ["python", "my_sim.py", "{{params_file}}"]. To run the same study on your farm, change the launcher block to your launcher's command (see Launcher mode).

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Every number Signal Viewer computes for you – a spectrum, a filter, a derivative, a mean, a comparison, a coordinate conversion – is checked against a reference that does not come from the app: a closed-form result, a definition (WGS84) or an independent textbook computation.

The same cases run in the test suite on every change, and you can run them yourself on your own machine and installation:

signalviewer-cli validate                  # a line per case; exit code 0 = all within tolerance

docs.title: Notes on the conventions
docs.text:
• FFT shows the single-sided amplitude: a sine of amplitude A reads A when its frequency is on a frequency bin. Between bins the Hann window reads up to 1.4 dB (15 %) low (scalloping) – use Welch or a longer window when the exact amplitude of an off-bin tone matters. Signals with gaps are put on an even time grid first (V03); amplitudes then read low by about the share of time the gaps cover (Known limitations).
  • Welch is a one-sided power spectral density in unit²/Hz: integrating it over frequency gives the variance (V05).
  • Low- / high-pass filters are 4th-order Butterworth run forward and backward (zero phase, V09); the cut-off is the −3 dB point of the result (V06, V07). To reproduce a result in MATLAB or SciPy: filtfilt(butter(4, fd/(fs/2)), x) with fd ≈ 1.12 × the cut-off for a low-pass and 0.90 × for a high-pass (exactly: svcore.ops.zero_phase_design_cutoff). A plain filtfilt(butter(4, fc/(fs/2)), x) is at −6 dB at fc.
  • Mean, RMS, std: on evenly spaced samples, the plain sample statistics (std: population, as NumPy's default; MATLAB's std divides by N − 1). On uneven sampling they are weighted by time (V13), marked ⏱ in the Inspector.
  • Attitude: Euler angles in aerospace order (yaw, then pitch, then roll), body → NED as ArduPilot and PX4 log it (V22, V23).
